summary: For 7-8 year olds, the target skill is choosing a calculation method (mental, jottings, formal written algorithm, or calculator) and measuring tools by first READING the numbers or the object, rather than defaulting to the column algorithm for everything. 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, tens and ones unchanged), while 345+278 involves regrouping and is where a written method earns its effort. The assessable skill is the justification for the choice, not just the answer — since two methods can both reach 545. Learners also decide which representation fits (for example when an empty number line helps more than base-ten blocks), integrate a calculator as a checking tool with a reasonableness judgement, and match measuring tools to an object's size and precision.
misconceptions: Applies the formal written method to everything, even 345+200 or 300+300, because it is the 'proper' way — missing the faster mental route (EEF: not self-regulating)
Attempts a regrouping calculation like 345+278 in the head and drops a carry, misjudging when a written method is needed
Trusts a calculator answer without a reasonableness check
Chooses a measuring tool that doesn't fit the object — a 30 cm ruler for a room — ignoring range and cumulative error

activities.title: Method chooser: route each calculation
steps: Work through a stream of mixed calculations (e.g. 345+200, 300+300, 345+278), and for each one first decide out loud which method fits: do it in your head, jot it down, write it out as columns, or use a calculator.
For each, state WHY that method fits before solving — e.g. 'I can see +200, so the tens and ones don't change, so I'll do it in my head.'
Compare the effort: deliberately set out columns for 345+200 and notice how many steps that takes versus saying 545 straight away.
Deliberately choose the written column method for 345+278 and name why (there is regrouping / a carry to track) it is worth the extra effort.

For a given problem, also decide which representation would help most — for example when an empty number line is clearer than base-ten blocks — and say what about the problem makes that representation fit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into two piles: 'do in your head' and 'worth writing down', and explain what feature of the numbers put each one where it went.
activities.insight: Reading the numbers first and spotting their features (round hundreds vs messy regrouping) lets you pick the method or representation that costs least effort; the column algorithm is worth its effort precisely for the messy cases, not for every calculation.

activities.title: Calculator check: is that sensible?
steps: A calculator returns 623 for 345+278. Decide whether that answer is sensible WITHOUT redoing the exact calculation.
Estimate instead: 345 is about 350, 278 is about 280, so the total should be around 630 — use that to judge the calculator's answer.

Say aloud a quick reasonableness check for the result: rounding to size (≈630), and the last-digit check (5+8=13, so the ones digit should be 3 — 623 ends in 3). Confirm these checks ratify 623 rather than flag an error.
Practise choosing when a calculator is the sensible tool (awkward numbers, checking) versus when a mental or written method is faster.
activities.insight: A calculator answer should be checked for reasonableness rather than trusted blindly; estimating the rough size and the expected last digit is a quick way to show an answer is sensible or catch a wrong one, though passing these checks does not prove the answer is exactly right (for example, 633 would also pass both).

activities.title: Fit the measuring tool to the object
steps: Decide which tool to use to measure a pencil versus a room: a 30 cm ruler, or a metre stick / tape measure.
Explain why a 30 cm ruler is a poor choice for a room — it needs many placements, and each placement can add a little error that accumulates.
Match a few objects (book, desk, corridor, pencil) to the tool whose range and precision suits them, and name the reason each time.
activities.insight: The same 'read the job, then choose the tool' habit used for arithmetic applies to measuring: match the tool's range and precision to the object, and recognise that repeated placement of a short ruler can accumulate error.

activities.title: Argue the choice with a method-defaulting partner
steps: Work with a partner (or in-role tutor) who writes out columns for EVERYTHING, including 345+200, and argue the case for when a mental method is enough.
Respond when the partner springs a regrouping calculation (345+278): decide whether to upgrade to a written method and give your reason.

Answer prompts like: 'Give me a calculation where the column method really IS the best choice, and one where it would be silly', and 'For 345+278, why does writing it down help more than doing it in your head?'
activities.insight: Being able to justify a method choice — including when to upgrade to a written method for regrouping — is the self-regulating reasoning the skill is really about.

checkQuestion: Two children work out 345 + 200. One sets out the column method and carries carefully; the other just says '545' straight away. Who chose the better method for THIS calculation, and why? Now what about 345 + 278 — would your advice change?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, the tens and ones unchanged) so the column method is unnecessary work, while 345+278 involves regrouping and is where a written method earns its keep — a judgement driven by the NUMBERS, not a blanket 'always use columns'.
